ai-adb397617d.headline: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation led by UAE investors
ai-adb397617d.fulltext:
OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering.
The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised.
Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO.
OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.
Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.
The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public."
Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering. In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation.

ai-1abb7be22e.headline: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump
ai-1abb7be22e.fulltext:
The latest shudder for stocks in the AI industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran.
The S&P 500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.
AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.
Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.
Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.
Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it was creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.
Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.
The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.
CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.
The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.
Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.
Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.
Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.
But US yields nevertheless fell sharply on Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.
The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.
Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.
That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.
Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.
CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expected “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86.

global-economics-8b0c156fef.headline: DeepSeek raises $15 billion to challenge Anthropic, OpenAI and other US AI labs
global-economics-8b0c156fef.fulltext:
BloombergPublished22 Oct 2026, 11:50 AM IST
(Bloomberg) -- The Chinese AI pioneer DeepSeek has raised about 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) in its latest fundraising round, one of the country’s largest ever and a sign of the startup’s ambitions to compete globally with the likes of Anthropic PBC and OpenAI.
The Hangzhou-based firm boosted its financing target at least twice as it talked with investors, from 50 billion yuan to 80 billion yuan before reaching the final tally, according to people familiar with the matter. Battery pioneer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. and WeChat-operator Tencent Holdings Ltd. were among the biggest investors in the round, said the people, asking not to be named as the details aren’t public.
DeepSeek’s funding sets the stage for one of the most highly anticipated Chinese market debuts in years. The AI upstart triggered a $1 trillion meltdown in global markets in 2025 when it showed the ability to compete with Silicon Valley’s leaders at a fraction of the cost of their models, but it’s never had the financial resources of the US frontier labs.
The latest fundraising shows that imbalance is beginning to moderate, although it still has far less financial firepower than Anthropic and OpenAI, which have each raised more than $100 billion. Like rival Moonshot, DeepSeek is preparing for an initial public offering that would be an important milestone for Chinese markets, Bloomberg News has reported.
DeepSeek has begun to spend more aggressively to build out AI data centers and to develop more open-source models for use in China and abroad.
The firm has regularly rolled out high-performance, low-cost models that put pressure on its domestic competitors and gained customers in the US and other overseas markets. In September, for example, it dropped V4.1 Flash, setting off a drop in the share prices of local rivals MiniMax Group Inc. and Z.AI Co. DeepSeek, Tencent and CATL representatives didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment.
More broadly, companies from Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. to ByteDance Ltd. have introduced low-cost AI services, typically open-sourced so customers can modify them as needed.
One widely shared benchmark chart from Artificial Analysis sketched out what has been called the “DeepSeek death zone,” where competitors will struggle to survive if they can’t beat the firm’s performance or they can’t charge lower prices.

climate-energy-e628f884e1.headline: Grid Constraints Curtailed 119 GW of Renewables in India in September
climate-energy-e628f884e1.fulltext:
The Hormuz crisis is tightening…
Britain’s approval of the Jackdaw…
Grid, flexibility, and transmission constraints amid limited battery storage forced India to curtail as much as 118.6 gigawatts (GW) of solar and wind power capacity in September, data by India’s JMK Research & Analytics showed.
A total of 118.6 GW of renewable energy capacity was affected by curtailment last month, including 96.9 GW of solar and 21.7 GW of wind capacity, according to data from regulator Grid-India.
“Key reasons for RE curtailment include demand-generation mismatches, transmission constraints, limited storage and grid flexibility, and seasonal overlaps between high renewable output and moderate demand,” JMK Research & Analytics said.
The curtailed renewable energy was equivalent to 1.28% of total renewable energy generation in India last month.
Between May and August, curtailments in India surged fourfold compared to last year, as 44.6 GW of new solar capacity was added, pressuring transmission infrastructure and flexibility, according to JMK’s analysis.
The growing curtailments signal that the surge in India’s solar and wind power capacity is not being matched by adequate expansion of grids and transmission infrastructure, and battery storage to manage the discharge of renewable energy when it’s needed.
India’s record renewable power generation and solar output were overshadowed by curtailments in July and August when India experienced power availability shortages.
Over 4% of the solar power generated in July and August had to be curtailed because of grid and operational constraints, the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) said in a report earlier this month.
The solar curtailments came as India’s demand surged between July and September and coal plants were increasingly operating with critically low inventories.
To address curtailments and a lack of flexibility in renewable energy sources, India plans to introduce, from July 2027, a regulation requiring developers of solar and wind energy projects to have battery storage installed at the sites.

ai-ca13395dd2.headline: Is training AI on song lyrics fair use? US court weighs question as India proposes mandatory licensing
ai-ca13395dd2.fulltext:
On October 21, in a lawsuit brought by music publishers, Anthropic asked a US federal judge to rule that its use of copyrighted song lyrics to train its chatbot Claude constitutes ‘fair use’. US District Judge Eumi Lee heard arguments from both sides in San Jose but did not issue a ruling, Reuters reported.
This case was filed by Universal Music Group (UMG), Concord and ABKCO in 2023, and they alleged that Anthropic used lyrics from hundreds of songs by artists such as Beyoncé, the Rolling Stones and the Beach Boys for training Claude. Both sides have sought summary judgment, asking the court to decide the case, or specific legal issues, without a full trial.
Under US copyright law, the fair-use doctrine permits certain uses of copyrighted works without permission from rights holders. In contrast, India provides specific fair-dealing exceptions under Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957, instead of a general fair-use defence. The Indian government has proposed a mandatory licensing framework for AI training, but it is not yet law.
Anthropic, through its lawyer, Sonal Mehta of WilmerHale, argued that this usage would fall under fair use since the training leads to transformative new content. Further, on the point of market harm, she argued that AI does not reduce demand for song lyrics; in fact, UMG itself describes AI as a net positive for the industry.
The publishers, through their lawyer, Matt Oppenheim of Oppenheim + Zebrak, argued that this training harms songwriters as Anthropic uses the lyrics for generation of competing content. He said users made nearly 120,000 requests to Claude to generate ‘synthetic lyrics’ over six months, and that models like Claude “could overwhelm the market with AI-generated content very easily”.
Judge Lee pressed both sides on fair use and the claim that Claude has the ability to write lyrics which would threaten the publishers in the market, Reuters reported.
Two other judges in the Northern District of California reached different conclusions in 2025 about whether AI training qualifies as fair use, Reuters noted. In 2025, now-retired Judge William Alsup had ruled that while pirated copies are not allowed for training, using lawfully acquired books to train AI models could qualify as fair use. Then, Judge Vince Chhabria, in a similar suit, ruled that AI training in many cases does not count as fair use.
Anthropic also faces lawsuits involving song lyrics brought by Sony Music Publishing and Round Hill Music.
On December 8, 2025, in Part I of a working paper about generative AI and copyright, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) proposed a mandatory blanket licence, dubbed “one nation, one licence, one payment”. According to this, lawfully accessed works cannot be withheld by rights holders. Instead, they would be granted royalties as decided by a government-appointed committee when the AI system is commercialised. The working paper was opened for public comments and indicated that a Part II would follow. MediaNama could not find this Part II.
Meanwhile, Indian courts have yet to resolve the legality of using copyrighted works to train AI models; the ANI v OpenAI case, with Indian Music Industry (IMI), T-Series and Saregama as intervenors, about ChatGPT’s training, is still pending.
MediaNama has sought comment from Anthropic, the publishers’ counsel and IMI. This story will be updated when they respond.

work-careers-429b8092a7.headline: India's GCCs offer up to 40% salary premium for AI talent as fresher hiring share declines
work-careers-429b8092a7.fulltext:
The change is also becoming visible in compensation. Industry estimates suggest that GCCs pay 15–30% more than traditional Indian IT services companies for comparable roles, with substantially higher premiums for specialised skills.
India's Global Capability Centres (GCCs) are increasingly favouring experienced professionals over fresh graduates, even as companies offer salary premiums of up to 40% to attract specialised artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity and engineering talent.
Hiring data from foundit shows that the share of entry-level professionals in GCC recruitment has declined from 42% to 30%, while the share of employees with four to six years of experience has risen from 26% to 34%. The shift comes as automation reduces the need for certain routine technology roles and global companies look for professionals capable of developing and deploying AI systems.
According to TeamLease Digital, specialised technology professionals can earn 30–40% more than those in comparable roles, particularly when they have the expertise to deploy AI at scale and deliver measurable business outcomes.
GCC hiring shifts towards experienced talent
The preference for experienced professionals is becoming more pronounced as GCCs take on complex responsibilities across global product development, technology infrastructure, analytics and engineering.
Neeti Sharma, CEO, TeamLease Digital, said mid-to-senior professionals accounted for over 77% of GCC hiring in FY26, compared with 60% in 2023.
"AI is reducing demand for routine coding roles while increasing demand for AI architects and specialised engineers. Freshers will continue to find opportunities, but practical, job-ready skills will matter more," Sharma said.
The trend is also reflected in foundit's hiring data. Professionals with four to six years of experience now account for 34% of GCC hiring, compared with 26% previously, while the entry-level share has declined from 42% to 30%.
Anupama Bhimrajka, VP – Marketing, foundit, said GCCs are placing greater emphasis on candidates who can take ownership of complex responsibilities and contribute with relatively less training.
The change does not necessarily indicate that GCCs are shutting out fresh graduates. Rather, the nature of entry-level opportunities is changing as routine tasks become increasingly susceptible to automation.
Abhilash Raghavan, CEO, SecondHQ, an NLB Services company, said hiring in 2026 is increasingly focused on specialised capabilities rather than volume, as organisations balance workforce expansion with automation and productivity goals.
According to Raghavan, candidates with four to ten years of experience account for a substantial share of demand, although freshers are still expected to represent around 16% of hiring under his estimates.
AI specialists command up to 40% salary premium
As GCCs become more selective, compensation is increasingly being determined by specialised capabilities rather than experience alone.
Sharma said AI and machine learning roles command some of the highest salaries, followed by data engineering, cloud and cybersecurity. Professionals possessing specialised expertise can earn 30–40% more than employees in comparable roles.
Raghavan estimates that employers may offer premiums of 20–35% for highly specialised AI talent, particularly in generative AI, large language models and machine learning operations. Cybersecurity and cloud security professionals also command higher salaries, depending on their experience and the availability of relevant skills.
foundit's estimates suggest that the premium can be particularly significant in AI and machine learning, where mid-career salaries range from ₹25.3 lakh to ₹45.3 lakh annually, while senior professionals can earn between ₹50.1 lakh and over ₹90 lakh.
Product management professionals with senior-level experience can command between ₹38.4 lakh and over ₹80 lakh, while senior data engineering and data science positions offer ₹42.1–75 lakh.
Cybersecurity professionals at the senior level can earn between ₹38.2 lakh and ₹70 lakh annually, according to foundit's estimates.
The demand for these capabilities is also growing faster than for conventional IT roles.
According to foundit, AI, data science and analytics accounted for 18% of GCC hiring and registered 38% year-on-year growth. By comparison, IT and software development, despite accounting for a larger 31% share of hiring, recorded 14% growth.
Engineering and product R&D represented another 16% of hiring, while cloud and cybersecurity contributed 11%.
How much do GCC employees earn in India?
Salary benchmarks from the three companies indicate that GCC compensation varies considerably by experience, specialisation and the global responsibilities attached to a role.
According to foundit's 2026 estimates, entry-level GCC employees with up to three years of experience earn between ₹5.4 lakh and ₹10.2 lakh annually. Mid-level professionals with four to eight years of experience earn ₹11.2–30.2 lakh, while senior employees with nine to fifteen years of experience command ₹23.2–58.2 lakh.
Leadership salaries typically begin at approximately ₹50 lakh and can exceed ₹1.5 crore.
TeamLease Digital places the entry-level salary range at ₹8–15 lakh, rising to ₹18–30 lakh for mid-level employees and ₹35–65 lakh for senior professionals. Leadership compensation can exceed ₹1.8 crore.
SecondHQ's estimates indicate an even wider compensation ceiling, with senior professionals earning ₹25–70 lakh and leadership packages ranging from ₹50 lakh to ₹3 crore or more.
The figures also show how salary growth differs across experience levels.
foundit's year-on-year GCC salary benchmarks indicate average growth of 15.6% for entry-level compensation ranges, compared with 10.4% for mid-level professionals and 3.8% for senior employees. Leadership compensation recorded an estimated 11% increase.
Sharma, meanwhile, expects average GCC salary increments of 10.4% in 2026, compared with 9.9% last year.
These benchmarks point to continued salary growth, although the strongest compensation gains are increasingly linked to specialised technical capabilities.
GCCs pay up to 30% more than IT services firms
The competition for specialised talent has also allowed GCCs to maintain a compensation advantage over traditional Indian IT services companies.
Sharma estimates that GCCs typically pay 20–30% more than IT services firms for comparable roles, with the gap remaining broadly stable.
Raghavan places the difference at 15–22%, saying that the premium appears to be stabilising after sharper increases in previous years.
foundit's benchmarks suggest a broader premium of 15–25% for comparable technology roles. However, the difference can increase to 30–40% for AI and generative AI positions, 25–35% for cybersecurity and 20–30% for product management.
Bhimrajka cautioned that it would be premature to conclude whether the overall GCC compensation advantage is widening or narrowing, given the lack of consistent year-on-year data comparing equivalent roles.
What is becoming clearer, according to industry executives, is that GCCs are no longer offering higher compensation uniformly. Instead, the premium is increasingly concentrated in roles requiring specialised expertise, functional ownership and business-critical responsibilities.
AI-related roles projected to account for 64% of GCC hiring demand in 2026
The change in recruitment priorities comes against a backdrop of continued employment growth across India's GCC sector.
According to the foundit Insights Tracker, GCC hiring demand is projected to reach 5.10 lakh opportunities in calendar year 2026, an increase of 12% from approximately 4.54 lakh in 2025.
The platform estimates that India had approximately 2,120 GCCs by June 2026, compared with around 2,000 in 2025.
More significantly, foundit projects that AI-related roles will account for 64% of GCC hiring demand in 2026, compared with 58.1% in 2025 and 11% in 2021.
The figures reflect how AI capabilities are becoming increasingly relevant across technology and business functions, although AI-related positions are not necessarily limited to employees developing AI models.
Employment forecasts from other staffing companies also point towards continued expansion, although their estimates cover different periods.
TeamLease Digital expects GCCs to add four to six lakh professionals over the next two to three years. SecondHQ estimates approximately 1.5–6 lakh new roles in FY27.
The figures are not directly comparable with foundit's projected 5.10 lakh hiring opportunities in calendar year 2026, which measures recruitment demand rather than net employment additions.
The broader direction, however, is consistent across the three companies: GCCs are expected to continue expanding their Indian operations, but hiring will increasingly favour professionals with specialised technical expertise and experience in managing complex business functions.
For fresh graduates, this raises the bar for entry into the sector. For experienced technology professionals, particularly those working across AI, data engineering and cybersecurity, it creates an opportunity to command higher compensation.
As automation changes the nature of work handled by GCCs, the industry's next phase of employment growth may depend less on the number of positions created and more on the capabilities companies are willing to pay for.

indian-startups-460b4305ee.headline: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance
indian-startups-460b4305ee.fulltext:
In his new book “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” writer Paris Marx examines how local communities are resisting the growing demand for water to cool data centers.
After ChatGPT was released in November 2022, the tech industry was quick to herald the chatbot as the marker of a new wave of technological progress. As companies pushed to create more powerful AI models, the water demand of their ambitions took a while to become clear. In April 2023, a research paper out of the University of California estimated that training the large language model behind the initial version of ChatGPT had required 185,000 gallons of water. For every extended conversation someone had with the chatbot or every time they asked it to write an email, they were effectively pouring a bottle of water down the drain.
That statistic got a lot of play when it was released. It became an early warning sign of what was coming as companies pushed chatbots as a universal technology that could replace psychologists, educators, lawyers, and even people’s friends or partners.
As public concern grew, Google and OpenAI came out with their own figures. The companies suggested that querying one of their chatbots used mere drops of water. Independent researchers were not impressed, arguing the companies were taking a narrow view of the water use necessary to power and cool increasingly monstrous data centers. Those water demands can be quite significant too.
A hyperscale data center can suck up between 1 and 5 million gallons of water a day, comparable to the amount used by a city of 10,000 to 50,000 people — depending on the part of the world we’re talking about. Consider how these companies often cluster data centers together and it becomes obvious what a challenge it can be to supply them.
Data centers end up competing with communities over their potable water supply.
The water demands of individual data centers are also continuing to grow. It’s not just that they need more water for cooling as they become larger and contain more servers. The graphics processing units (GPUs) that power generative AI are much more resource-intensive than the chips and storage devices that traditionally filled data center racks. GPUs run harder and throw off more heat, meaning they also need more energy or water to keep them cool.
Data centers cannot just use any kind of water either; it has to be clean enough to ensure the equipment and pipes are not damaged. Tapping into public drinking water is both easier and cheaper than paying the cost of treatment themselves. That means data centers end up competing with communities over their potable water supply.
If we want to look at a part of the world where the issue of data center water use has taken center stage, there are few better countries to turn to than Chile. In October 2019, mass social demonstrations broke out across the country. One of the movement’s driving slogans was about water. It was poor timing for Google as it was fighting for approval and public support of its latest data center project, a $200 million data center project in Cerrillos, on the southwest side of Santiago.
The company made a pitch similar to the one residents in communities the world over have heard whenever a data center is proposed: that the facility would bring jobs and prosperity, and give the area a leg up on further tech investments. The reality was not so straightforward. Google’s new data center would bring a lot of short-term construction jobs but not much long-term employment. And it would need a lot of water — something Cerrillos did not have much of to spare.
Local residents were not as passive as the company had hoped. A group of concerned citizens established an organization called MOSACAT, which stands for Community Socio-Environmental Movement for Water and Land, and started poring over whatever information they could get their hands on to try to understand what the project would mean for them. “Usually these reports use quite technical language, and this is a working- class community where not many people are lawyers, for example, or experts on ecology,” explains Sebastián Lehuedé, a researcher at King’s College London who is from Chile and spent time in Cerrillos.
Data center companies claim they will be respectful and considerate neighbors, but too often hide the extent of the damage from the scale of their demands on local resources.
According to its own projections, the data center Google wanted to build in Cerrillos was poised to use 169 liters of water every single second. In just one day, the data center would consume as much water as all 80,000 residents of Cerrillos use for drinking in a year. To make matters worse, it wanted to draw that water from an underground aquifer that had been under a decree that restricted how much water could be removed since 2005. Just weeks before the project was rubber-stamped by the environmental authority, that decree had been upgraded to a complete prohibition on new extraction.
The water use estimates set off alarm bells for the residents. Chile had already been in an unprecedented drought since 2010. By 2021, more than half the country’s 19 million residents lived in areas experiencing severe water scarcity, forcing hundreds of rural communities to rely on tankers to deliver drinking water.
The local activists ultimately built the case against one of the largest companies on the planet. After months of meetings and advocacy to spread awareness, they were able to put a referendum question to the residents of Cerrillos about the project in December 2019. The results were damning: 49% of voters chose to reject the project, while 38% wanted it to go forward.
After both the municipality and community members filed claims against Google in 2020, the company returned with a new proposal in February 2022. It offered to cool the data center exclusively with air-conditioning rather than with water.
Across the city in Quilicura, opposition was building too. Microsoft announced its intention to build a data center in the community in 2022, the same year strict water-rationing rules had come into effect in Santiago. As in Cerrillos, residents were worried that another large data center would threaten their access to water and provide little in return.
Vicente Bardales, a member of the Quilicura Socio Environmental Resistance group, told Rest of World that the companies touch down in places like Quilicura only to “use water, [and] dry up the territory, but don’t give anything back to the population.”
Only a tiny proportion of water in Uruguay is used for human consumption.”
Similar scenarios to that of Chile played out across Latin America. The following year, the Uruguayan capital of Montevideo found itself under a state of emergency as the country was hit by its worst drought in 70 years. As residents demonstrated against the misuse of water by industry, they found out Google was planning a data center in Canelones, a little less than an hour north of Montevideo.
“Only a tiny proportion of water in Uruguay is used for human consumption,” explained Daniel Pena, a researcher at University of the Republic. “The majority is used for big agro industries, such as soya, rice, and wood pulping. Now we have Google planning to use enormous quantities of water.” Pena had to go to court to get details of its planned water use from the Ministry of Environment, ultimately finding Google’s 72-acre site was planning to use 2 million gallons of water each day to power its cooling systems.
Uruguayans had fought for fresh drinking water to be considered a basic right in the national constitution two decades earlier, and as companies like Google moved in, they feared its realization was slipping from their grasp.
Uruguayans suspected Google had shifted its focus to their country because it had run into such opposition in Chile. Neighboring Brazil already has over 180 data centers, even as many regions regularly experience drought conditions. On the outskirts of Fortaleza, Brazil’s fourth-largest city, at least four major data centers were looking to set up shop to take advantage of a free-trade zone in the municipality of Caucaia. One in particular would be the size of 12 football fields, costing an estimated $10 billion, and though it will technically be owned by a local wind energy company, it is actually being developed to serve TikTok. This is in a region that experienced emergency drought conditions for 16 of the 21 years between 2003 and 2024.
What Cerillos, Canelones, and Caucaia are experiencing is increasingly a global phenomenon. Around the world, data center companies claim they will be respectful and considerate neighbors, but too often they hide the extent of the damage that follows from the scale of their demands on local resources. This is particularly acute in parts of the Global South, but the effects are now also being felt across the United States and Europe.

ai-5cabb389fd.headline: Recursive shows first result of its AI-driven research process with Flint
ai-5cabb389fd.fulltext:
Recursive shows first result of its AI-driven research process with Flint
Key Points
- The AI startup Recursive has released Flint, a language model for programming tasks that was developed largely by an internal AI system called "Eureka Machine."
- Flint uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 40 billion parameters (2.5 billion active) and is optimized for fast local execution on Apple and Nvidia hardware.
- The model is freely available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Recursive's long-term goal is to use this approach to create AI systems that can take charge of their own further development.
AI startup Recursive built its first language model with an AI system that proposes, runs, and evaluates its own experiments.
AI startup Recursive has released Flint, its first language model. An AI system called "Eureka Machine" was involved in nearly every step of development, proposing ideas on its own, building them out, testing them, and planning follow-up experiments based on the results.
Flint is a mixture-of-experts model (MoE) designed for agentic coding on local hardware, and it was built in four months. Out of 40 billion total parameters, only 2.5 billion are active per token. Recursive claims Flint leads coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Pro v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SWE-Bench Verified among MoE models (such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Laguna S 2.1) with fewer than 50 billion parameters. The results haven't been independently verified yet.
The model is meant to compete with dense models in the 25 to 40 billion parameter range while running more than five times faster. On a MacBook Pro with M4 Pro, Flint generates more than 125 tokens per second at short contexts, according to Recursive. On an Nvidia RTX Spark with 64 GB of memory, it tops 150. Compared to similar models, inference is up to twice as fast.
Eureka Machine chose the architecture, quantization, and compute kernels on its own
Recursive says the Eureka Machine automates the entire research cycle, running multiple approaches in parallel. For Flint, it helped with training data, optimizers, architecture design, and inference tuning. Three examples show how the system shaped the model's performance.
Starting from an architecture with 35 billion total and 3 billion active parameters, the Eureka Machine tested different expert configurations. The final design of 40 billion total and 2.5 billion active parameters turned out to be the best tradeoff between speed and coding performance among all the variants it tested.
For quantization, the system went against common practice and reduced the output layer to four bits as well. An added distillation step was meant to recover the lost accuracy, and according to Recursive, it needed roughly half as many training steps as the previous method. The finished NVFP4 model sits only 0.7 points behind the 16-bit version across benchmarks.
The Eureka Machine also built specialized compute kernels for Apple Silicon and Nvidia RTX Spark. On Apple's M4 and M5 chips, a Metal megakernel combines the entire forward pass during token generation into a single operation. Recursive says these optimizations across multiple development stages are what enable the high inference speed.
Flint runs locally and ships with open weights
Flint supports context windows of up to 512,000 tokens, though Recursive recommends capping it at 256,000. The model weights are available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Supported runtimes include llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, and SGLang. Recursive also released rec, its own inference engine for Apple Silicon.
All of that means the model can run locally without sending code to external servers. Recursive does acknowledge that Flint needs more guidance on complex tasks than large proprietary coding models. The company recommends breaking bigger tasks into smaller steps.
Recursive is betting it can build AI that keeps building better AI
The startup, founded by Richard Socher and others including former DeepMind researcher Tim Rocktäschel, came out of stealth in May 2026 and raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation. At the time, Recursive had no concrete technical results to show. Flint is the company's first publicly available model from its automated research process.
The long-term goal is to build a superintelligence that keeps improving itself. Each new model is supposed to make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, so the next generation of models can be built faster and more efficiently. Eventually, Recursive wants to apply the same approach to automate research in other scientific fields.
Whether this will actually produce accelerating self-improvement is far from settled. Former Google DeepMind research lead Oriol Vinyals considers AI-assisted self-improvement realistic but thinks an intelligence explosion is unlikely. Finding good research ideas and reliably judging results remain especially hard problems for AI systems.
Other AI labs are already using AI to build new models too. Anthropic says Claude now handles a large share of its own development work, while OpenAI deploys AI agents across its entire research pipeline. How far that automation actually goes is still debated. A study of more than 700 task logs found that AI agents handle large portions of the work, but humans still make most of the critical research calls.
Those are the steps Recursive wants to automate with the Eureka Machine. Flint is a first concrete result, but it doesn't yet prove full recursive self-improvement. For that, the company would need to show that a model built with the Eureka Machine actually makes the Eureka Machine itself a better researcher.

deep-tech-50539c2e18.fulltext:

Unitree Robotics is developing a “self-evolving” feedback loop designed to allow humanoid robots to write code, run simulations and improve their real-world performance independently, founder Wang Xingxing said, in a move that mirrors a broader push towards “self-improving” artificial intelligence.
Speaking on Thursday at a physical AI conference hosted by Unitree in Hangzhou, Wang unveiled the project, dubbed “Unitree Rehearsal”, which he called the company’s most important initiative of the year.
The project sought to shift robotics development away from labour-intensive manual programming towards a continuous, autonomous feedback loop, he said. Under the system in development, AI would search research papers, write code and test it in simulations before running trials on physical robots.
While humans could still help assess performance and provide feedback, Wang said the ultimate goal was to create an automated cycle that could exponentially accelerate the development of robotics algorithms.
“In the past, every robotics engineer had to write code and debug manually, which is relatively inefficient,” Wang said. “As AI models improve, we expect them to take on more of the planning and iteration, reducing the need for human intervention.”
Leading AI companies had already begun using models to generate code and gather data under human guidance, Wang said, arguing that robotics firms could follow a similar blueprint. Unlike digital software, however, robots also had to navigate environmental unpredictability and mechanical errors, he said.
The comments came just days after Wang predicted that advances in OpenAI’s GPT-6 model could spur a broader robotics breakthrough within one to two years. His latest speech focused on the critical steps needed to translate AI model improvements into real-world utility.
In a video shown at the event, robots developed by Unitree used GPT-6 to map routes and plan movements without task-specific training, though the presentation did not demonstrate how consistently the machines could replicate that behaviour in unfamiliar environments.
While large AI models could handle robot planning and navigation, Wang said the biggest challenge was “aligning the AI model’s inputs and outputs with those of a real robot”.
If that challenge could be overcome, humanoid robots could be tidying rooms on command as early as 2027, Wang suggested, though he offered 2028 as a more realistic estimate.
Unitree’s upbeat road map echoed recent comments from Elon Musk. On Wednesday, the Tesla CEO told the US carmaker’s earnings call that humanoid robots could eventually become “the biggest product on Earth” and outnumber humans. He cautioned, however, that Tesla still faced about a year of development hurdles with its Optimus robot.
Data, however, points to a challenging transition from laboratory to living room. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index found that robots succeeded in only 12 per cent of real-world household tasks during evaluations, despite performing significantly better in simulation.

india-deep-tech-eef06c4646.headline: ITBP raises drone units to counter China, prepares for Galwan-like battles
india-deep-tech-eef06c4646.fulltext:
The Indo-Tibetan Border Police is significantly upgrading its capabilities with drone platoons, advanced training, and underground infrastructure to counter China's evolving military strategies along the Line of Actual Control.
Key Points
- ITBP has established drone platoons in all border units and is allocating significant funds for drone and anti-drone systems.
- A new 'Strike' course is being implemented to train personnel for Galwan-like combat scenarios, with full force training by the end of 2027.
- The force is constructing underground shelters along the border, adapting to lessons from modern warfare where above-ground structures are vulnerable.
- ITBP is modernising its weapons, vehicles, and improving troop comfort in sub-zero conditions to enhance operational preparedness.
- DG Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor emphasised the need to move beyond traditional warfare to effectively counter China, India's "biggest adversary."
The Indo-Tibetan Border Police has raised drone platoons in all its border units, prepared a new 'Strike' course to better handle Galwan-like battles and is creating underground infrastructure along the front "in a big way" as part of the new warfare to counter India's "biggest adversary" China, the force's chief said on Thursday.
ITBP director general (DG) Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor told his troops at a force base in Rajasthan's Alwar that countering China through "traditional" means of warfare was a thing of the past and hence they were investing in modernising the force, its weapons, vehicles and border posts.
The Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), raised in 1962, guards the 3,488-km-long Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China.
Modernising Border Defence Against China
The DG noted that the recent Ukraine-Russia and Iran-US wars have shown the importance of drone and anti-drone technology through which a small country can overwhelm a bigger nation during conflict.
Kapoor, who is set to retire from service on October 31, addressed his troops during an investiture ceremony held leading up to the force's 65th Raising Day on October 24.
He said the China front was our "most difficult" border, and China was a "powerful" neighbour and India's "biggest adversary," requiring enhanced capabilities to "counter" it.
"Drones have become a major challenge and an opportunity also. It will be difficult to compete with China using traditional methods... They have modernised and invested heavily in their PLA but drones are such that a small country can give a befitting contest to a bigger nation," he said.
He noted that almost 10,000-15,000 Russian troops are killed in the war with Ukraine every month.
"This is despite the fact that it (Russia) is a big country and a superpower. They (Russia) thought that they would capture (Ukraine) in 1-2 months but it is the fourth year counting, and every month they (Russians) have 10-15 thousand bodies reaching them," the DG said.
He added that this caused such "big damage" and that Russia was suffering because of that one decision.
Kapoor then cited the Iran-US war as an example, noting that Iran, without an Air Force, Navy, or Army, engaged in combat with the global superpower.
"The role of traditional armies has changed since the drones arrived, and we must embrace drone and anti-drone systems in a big way," he said.
Strategic Investment in Drone Technology
Kapoor said the approximately 95,000-personnel-strong, mountain-warfare-trained ITBP has received government funds worth Rs 400 crore and 70 percent of these funds have been earmarked for enhancing the force's drone warfare capabilities.
"Each border guarding battalion now has a drone platoon, and we are training drone pilots and building drones too."
"The Ministry of Home Affairs has also granted in-principle approval to a bigger modernisation scheme of Rs 4,000 crore, of which we will earmark Rs 1,000 crore for drone and anti-drone systems," the DG said.
Enhancing Combat Readiness and Infrastructure
He informed the troops that a new course named 'Strike' has been developed to train ITBP personnel, which will enhance their capabilities to face Galwan-like situations. The entire force will undergo this training by the end of 2027.
Chinese soldiers used stones, nail-studded sticks, iron rods and clubs while carrying out brutal attacks on Indian soldiers along the LAC at Galwan (Ladakh) in June, 2020 resulting in 20 casualties on the Indian side while China belatedly claimed only 4 of its troops were killed. Multiple reports suggested that the Chinese fatalities were much higher.
The ITBP chief added that a new combat team, the Shaurya commandos, has been raised. This team displayed its skills during the "ongoing" faceoff with the Chinese PLA troops at multiple places in Arunachal Pradesh.
These commandos will be in every border battalion and will give the force a distinct identity, he said.
Prioritising Troop Welfare and Future Capabilities
The DG said the force was constructing underground shelters (bunkers) at border locations "in a big way," learning from the lessons of the new warfare, as above-ground buildings can become a target in 'hot war' situations, indicating the post-Operation Sindoor conflict with Pakistan.
He said a pilot project is underway in this context and they plan to have these under-ground shelters in the coming years, equipped with the same comfort available in above-ground buildings.
Kapoor said the force also worked on the ensuring the comfort and operational prepardeness of the troops by insulating 342 out of 383 barracks present in areas which face "sub-zero" temperatures, has procured 141 generator sets to ensure electricity at remote troop locations and got solar water heaters installed at a number of such facilities.
"This will help enhance the morale and confidence of the troops and improve the ITBP's operational preparedness," he said.
The DG added that a 'cold start kit' was provided to border units which helps vehicles get immediate ignition in icy weather.
"Many years ago when we were in Kosovo in sub zero temperatures the vehicles there used to start in one crank. We wondered why this wasn't happening here? We did some experiments and now we can do it," he said.
The DG also asked his troops to keep fit and healthy, saying a new diet plan has been introduced in the force and the "very high" content of sugar and oil has been lessened.
He expressed concern over the cases of Alcohol Dependence Syndrome (ADS) in the ITBP which have doubled or tripled since 2020.
The DG also asked the troops to be cautious against ADS and 'honey trap' instances of being lured by someone into sharing sensitive information through the social media.
He added that the ITBP was also modernising its weapons, some of which are about 50 years old, and improving mobility through the procurement of new all-terrain Vehicles, ground vehicles and quick reaction vehicles,
We have prepared a plan to become a specialised high-altitude mountain fighting force through all these measures, Kapoor said.

The company’s three cofounders — CEO Arvind Lakshmikumar, CBO Ankit Kumar and chief commercial officer (CCO) Cecilia D’Souza — collectively pocketed ₹137.2 Cr from the defence tech company’s ₹852 Cr IPO. Cofounder Kumar, who serves as the CBO and CRO of Tonbo, offloaded 5.8 Lakh shares worth ₹40.6 Cr and continues to hold 24.6 Lakh shares. Meanwhile CCO D’Souza, offloaded around 2.3 Lakh shares for ₹16.1 Cr. The largest selling shareholders in Tonbo Imaging’s IPO were its related entities, Bengaluru-based CEAQ Technologies Pvt Ltd and Singapore-based CEAQ Technologies Pte Ltd. The cofounders are the directors of these aforementioned entities as well. While CEAQ Technologies Pvt Ltd offloaded its entire shareholding of around 50 Lakh shares for ₹350 Cr, the Singapore-based entity sold 41.6 Cr shares to rake in ₹291 Cr. The Singapore-based entity continues to retain 1.05 Cr post the IPO. Early Investors Cash In Among other shareholders, Artiman, an early-stage sector agnostic venture fund, has made ₹13.8 Cr by selling 2 Lakh shares, clocking a return multiple of 4.8X on its investment. It will retain another 2 Lakh shares, valued at ₹13.8 Cr at the upper price band. Amit Dilip Shah, who is a partner at Artiman, individually sold 84,000 shares for ₹5.9 Cr at ₹700 apiece, translating to a 4.1X return, while his remaining 1.4 Lakh shares are worth ₹9.8 Cr. The company's operating revenue declined 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹469.1 Cr in FY25. Net profit fell to ₹50.8 Cr from ₹72.8 Cr in the previous year. Investors bidding for 115.87 Cr shares against the 85.26 Lakh shares on offer. The allotment of shares materialised today. indian-startups-8dc3e50fc7.headline: CureBay Bags ₹100 Cr To Scale Rural Clinics Network, Enhance AI Screening Offerings
indian-startups-8dc3e50fc7.fulltext: Healthtech startup CureBay raised around ₹100 Cr ($10.6 Mn) in a pre-Series C funding round, comprising over ₹69 Cr in equity led by IvyCap Ventures alongside existing investors and around ₹30 Cr in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners. CureBay cofounder and CEO Priyadarshi Mohapatra told Inc42 that the round came amid strong investor interest. The startup will use the proceeds to expand geographically, strengthen its delivery network and invest in its AI and technology capabilities. The healthtech startup, which currently operates in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Bihar, plans to enter Telangana and Andhra Pradesh markets next. It aims to grow its network of rural clinics from 250 to 800 over the next two to three years. CureBay connects patients in underserved areas with healthcare providers through a combination of rural clinics, local community health workers and a digital platform linking patients to doctors, hospitals, diagnostic laboratories and pharmacies. It also uses AI-assisted screening and care coordination to support patient care. The startup is also investing in GPUs and training AI models to screen patients and assess health risks. Its existing AI products cover areas such as skin conditions, dental health and haemoglobin screening, with plans to expand these capabilities. “We have a full suite of AI products for areas like skin, dental, and haemoglobin. We will keep adding more products and continue investing in width as well as depth,” Mohapatra said. CureBay also runs Kavach, a subscription programme designed to encourage preventive care by offering consultations and support for medicines, diagnostics and certain hospitalisation-related costs. The startup claims to have served over 12 Lakh patients and connected more than 270 doctors and 1,000 healthcare professionals across 4,500 pincodes. Prior to this round, CureBay had raised over $34.6 Mn from investors including Bertelsmann India Investments, British International Investment and Elevar Equity. While the startup is yet to file its audited FY26 financial statements, Mohapatra said it closed the fiscal year with an annual recurring revenue (ARR) of nearly ₹170 Cr. Mohapatra attributed the growth to customers spending more on CureBay as they increasingly view it as a trusted healthcare partner, alongside the expansion into new markets. A KsheerasagarPublished22 Oct 2026, 06:58 PM IST Domestic technology stocks have staged a strong turnaround in October after suffering heavy losses, as better-than-expected September-quarter performance, attractive valuations, and fears of a global AI slowdown have prompted investors to turn their attention back to software stocks, making the Nifty IT index a standout performer. Infosys gained 16%, while HCL Technologies advanced 15.5%. The rally follows a global selloff in software stocks earlier this year, as some investors feared that AI could disrupt their business models. Slowing revenue growth amid geopolitical concerns and rising client demand for lower prices also sapped investor sentiment. Amid strong support from heavyweight stocks, the Nifty IT index advanced 16% and reclaimed the 30,000 mark, touching its highest level in eight months last week. agritech-da64b71f1c.headline: Odisha to unveil India's 1st dedicated Agri-PV policy, targets 1 GW by 2030
agritech-da64b71f1c.fulltext:
Odisha to unveil India's 1st dedicated Agri-PV policy, targets 1 GW by 2030
The proposed policy will allow farming alongside solar power generation, ensure 90 per cent of project land remains cultivated and offer farmers new income opportunities
Listen to This Article
Odisha will soon unveil its agrivoltaics policy that will facilitate agricultural cultivation alongside solar power generation on the same land, making it the first state in India to introduce a separate policy framework for the emerging sector.
The proposed Agri-PV Policy 2026 targets the installation of 1 gigawatt (GW) of agrivoltaic capacity by 2030, while safeguarding farmers’ interests through provisions requiring at least 90 per cent of project land to remain under active cultivation.
Deputy Chief Minister Kanak Vardhan Singh Deo, who also holds the Agriculture and Farmers’ Empowerment and Energy portfolios, announced the proposed policy while delivering the keynote address at the ministerial session of the 7th Agrivoltaics World Conference 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Thursday.
"The policy is being designed around the principle of 'One Field, Two Harvests,' allowing farmers to continue growing crops while generating electricity from solar panels installed above agricultural fields. The state government plans to ensure that the expansion of renewable energy does not come at the cost of agricultural land or farmers’ livelihoods," he said.
According to the policy framework outlined by the deputy chief minister, agricultural land used for agrivoltaic projects would retain its agricultural classification, and farmers would remain eligible for crop insurance under the proposed safeguards.
Also Read
The requirement that at least 90 per cent of project sites remain under active cultivation will help distinguish agrivoltaics from conventional ground-mounted solar installations, where land is primarily used for power generation.
The proposed policy is expected to provide farmers with two broad participation models. They could invest in and own agrivoltaic systems themselves, earning income from both agricultural produce and electricity generation, or enter into partnerships with solar developers in return for assured long-term lease rentals. These options will enable farmers to benefit from the clean energy transition without necessarily having to bear the entire investment burden.
Odisha is proposing 25-year power purchase agreements with GRIDCO, along with guaranteed power offtake, grid connectivity and open-access rights to attract private investment and provide greater revenue certainty to project developers. These provisions will create a predictable commercial framework for agrivoltaic projects, which require coordination between agricultural operations, solar infrastructure and electricity distribution.
The proposed policy also seeks to integrate agrivoltaic incentives with existing agricultural support systems, including drip irrigation, solar-powered pumps, cold storage and agro-processing facilities. The state government aims to develop a model that delivers benefits beyond electricity generation by linking renewable energy generation with improvements in farm productivity and post-harvest infrastructure.
Addressing the conference, Singh Deo emphasised that the farmer would remain the primary beneficiary of the initiative, with solar infrastructure serving as a means of supplementing agricultural incomes rather than replacing farming. “We want to make our farmers empowered from Annadata (food provider) to Urjadata (power producer),” he said.
The state also plans to utilise agrivoltaics as a potential climate adaptation strategy amid rising temperatures and increasingly erratic rainfall. Climate projections for Odisha indicate mounting challenges for agriculture by 2070, making the development of farming systems that can withstand heat stress and changing precipitation patterns increasingly important.
Raised solar panels can create partially shaded microclimates that help reduce heat exposure, conserve soil moisture and protect crops against excessive solar radiation, depending on the crop, panel configuration and local climatic conditions. The structures can also provide some protection for agricultural workers against direct sunlight.
Odisha has already secured clean energy investment commitments worth Rs 67,000 crore, covering projects with a combined proposed capacity of 6.8 GW at its renewable energy investor conclave in February 2026. The government is now planning to extend this investment momentum to agrivoltaics, an area that could bring renewable energy development more directly into the agricultural economy.
"Preparatory work has already begun on the ground, with a 1 MW agrivoltaic project under implementation. The state is also pursuing a pilot collaboration with Singapore's Nanyang Technological University to test advanced agrivoltaic technologies and assess their suitability for Odisha's agricultural conditions," Singh Deo said and invited international research institutions, private investors and other states to collaborate with Odisha in developing a farmer-centred agrivoltaics model.
Odisha has around 4.07 million acres of cropland considered suitable for agrivoltaic development, in addition to approximately 4.77 million acres of fallow land. While the proposed policy emphasises retaining cultivation on project sites, assessments of land suitability, crop compatibility, water availability and grid infrastructure will be key in identifying commercially viable locations.

world-3da0d07e19.fulltext:
[Text below is The Economic Times's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Artificial intelligence could boost global growth, but poorer countries, smaller companies and younger workers risk missing out unless access to power, digital infrastructure and skills improves, according to officials from the IMF and OECD.
The warning comes as massive investment in chips and AI infrastructure has helped support global growth and drive stock markets to record highs, while raising concerns about whether companies can generate sufficient returns on large spending commitments as borrowing costs rise.
"For many developing economies, the critical question is whether they can adopt and diffuse AI," Era Dabla-Norris, deputy director of the International Monetary Fund's Fiscal Affairs Department, told the Reuters Global Markets Forum.
Effective AI adoption could add up to 0.5% to annual global growth over the medium term, the IMF estimates.
"But the aggregate productivity evidence, so far, is much less," Dabla-Norris said.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development estimates AI could add 0.4% to 1.2% to annual productivity growth across its member countries. But its chief economist, Stefano Scarpetta, said that workplace use trails consumer use, with only limited adoption in core business functions.
"There is a large gap between exposure and actual use," Scarpetta said.
The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide could be exposed to AI, as reports of mass layoffs gather pace.
Barclays said it was cutting around 5,000 jobs this year as it uses technology including AI to reduce costs and improve returns. EBay is reported to be laying off 9% of its workforce, while Qualcomm is expected to cut jobs globally in a "performance-focused reduction".
Dabla-Norris said younger and entry-level workers could be particularly vulnerable if AI takes over tasks through which employees traditionally gain experience.
Synopsis
Recent conversations underscore the transformative possibilities of artificial intelligence in fostering global economic growth and improving productivity. Nevertheless, challenges in accessing this technology persist for less affluent nations and smaller enterprises. Additionally, youth and entry-level workers might experience increased job insecurity due to AI's workplace disruptions. As corporations initiate workforce reductions to adapt to AI, effective adoption of this technology will be vital in creating fair growth prospects moving forward.

world-886f221d73.headline: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump
world-886f221d73.fulltext:
Options trader Anthony Spina works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Wednesday, Jan. 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Richard Drew, File)
NEW YORK (AP) — The latest shudder for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran.
The S&P 500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the U.S. market, where the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.
AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.
Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.
It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4% surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment.
Another pullback in AI stocks sent the S&P 500 to its worst day in three months.
Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.
Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.
Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.
The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.
CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.
The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.
Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.
Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.
Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.
But U.S. yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.
Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.
That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the U.S. stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.
Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses Thursday.
CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89 to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00 to 26,008.86.

world-535986e68c.fulltext:
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that President Vladimir Putin hasn’t yet named a negotiating team for prospective trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S.
Ukraine and Russia have signaled their willingness to resume U.S.-backed peace talks to seek an end to the war, but deep disagreements over territory and security guarantees underscore the obstacles ahead. Kyiv residents were mostly pessimistic about the latest developments surrounding peace negotiations. (AP video by Dan Bashakov)
Russian forces attacked Kyiv with a barrage of missiles and drones overnight into Thursday, killing one person and injuring at least 22 others, as strikes hit residential areas and damaged infrastructure, local authorities said. (AP video by Dan Bashakov)
Russian drone attacks on residential areas and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv region killed one person and injured at least 13 others, emergency officials said.
Rescue workers put out a fire at a residential house destroyed in a Russian missile strike on Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka)

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles in an hourslong nighttime barrage, while the Russian military said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted over 800 drones fired by Ukraine at Moscow and other cities.
At least four people were killed in Ukraine and dozens of others were wounded, officials said, in the attacks that began only hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations between Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
“Russia has not changed the way it wages this war, and it is taking no steps that would signal a genuine desire to end it,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after the barrage.
Putin’s consent came in talks in St. Petersburg with U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, who spoke of a “new momentum” toward peace after meeting Tuesday with Zelenskyy in Norway. The talks are supposed to start sometime after Nov. 10. No date was set.
Speaking with reporters, Vice President Vance says Russia and Ukraine have agreed to return to the negotiating table after progress by Trump envoy Steve Witkoff.
Representatives of the three countries held rounds of “technical” talks in the United Arab Emirates and Switzerland in January and February, seeking to lay the groundwork for detailed negotiations. But they reported little progress beyond exchanges of prisoners of war. Russia and Ukraine remain far apart in their terms for stopping the fighting despite U.S. efforts.
The U.S. has proposed the United Arab Emirates as a possible location for the new talks, said Zelenskyy, who has said only a meeting of leaders can end the deadlock.
Russia’s aerial attacks hit 12 regions of Ukraine overnight, killing at least four people and wounding scores of others, including five children, Zelenskyy said on social media Thursday.
Two women, ages 50 and 60, were killed and dozens of other people were wounded in a Russian strike on a market in Lozova, in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv region, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration. Another person was killed in other strikes on Kharkiv, the State Emergency Service said.
The Ukrainian capital endured a noisy night as 21 ballistic missiles came in three waves, Zelenskyy said, smashing apartment buildings, energy facilities, a railway station and the Kyiv subway system, shopping malls and businesses. One person was killed in Kyiv.
The Russian attack on Kyiv included three ballistic missiles carrying cluster munitions — bombs that open in the air and release scores of smaller bomblets, Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainians are bracing for the bitterly cold months ahead as the recent escalation in Russian attacks targets the power grid to deny civilians heat, light and running water. Ukraine says Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for an annual campaign Ukrainians describe as “ weaponizing winter.”
Since Oct. 11, Russia has launched 170 strikes on Ukraine’s critical energy facilities, Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader has pleaded with Washington to supply more Patriot air-defense ammunition to stop the missiles, and to heap more sanctions on Russia to pressure Moscow to pursue peace.
Instead, Trump has agreed with Putin to import diesel from Russia and waived heavy sanctions on Moscow, while U.S. officials say Patriot ammunition is in short supply.
“Russia is clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air defense supplies from our partners,” Zelenskyy said. “It is equally clear that when some partners ease the pressure on Russia, it only reinforces Putin’s belief that his goals are within reach.”
Western analysts say Putin wants to cut out Europe and Kyiv and negotiate Ukraine’s future directly with Washington. The Trump administration has also disparaged Europe.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Putin had received an invitation to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December but hasn’t yet decided whether to go.
“The American administration is doing a lot to help a peaceful settlement,” Peskov told reporters. “European capitals are doing nothing to promote a peaceful resolution, and they are doing a great deal to provoke the further escalation of fighting.”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would “be represented at the highest level” at the summit if Trump invites the country.
“Let’s hope that this is possible. So far we have not received such a signal. We are counting on it,” he said at a news conference with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo in Kyiv.
Witkoff, the Trump envoy who met Wednesday with Putin in St. Petersburg, was harshly criticized in Ukraine and the U.S. for praising the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” after he released a retired American teacher who was imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
Assassination attempts against Putin’s foes — routinely denied by the Kremlin — have been common during his decades in power. And as the five-year anniversary of Russia’s all-out invasion of its neighbor approaches, aerial strikes have killed thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of soldiers on both sides.
The latest “brutal” Russian attacks demonstrate “what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. “Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses overnight downed 808 Ukrainian drones, with two people reported wounded.
Moscow’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 630 of the drones were fired toward the Russian capital between late Wednesday and early Thursday. Moscow airports temporarily restricted air traffic overnight.
The Russian military hit facilities involved in making and storing drones and cruise missiles, as well as striking transport infrastructure in Kyiv, the Defense Ministry said. Infrastructure in the southern port of Odesa and vessels used for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it said.
In other developments, the bodies of 252 people, said by Russia to be Ukrainian soldiers, were returned to Ukraine in an exchange, Ukraine’s agency for prisoners of war said Thursday.
Russia received 25 bodies of Russian soldiers, Russian lawmaker Shamsail Saraliyev, a member of a parliamentary group overseeing the exchanges, told the RBC news outlet.
