world-db746dbf03.headline: First human case of Shamonda virus detected in France, officials say
world-db746dbf03.fulltext:
First human case of Shamonda virus detected in France, officials say
- Published
The first known human case of the Shamonda virus (Shav) has been detected in a patient who died in early October, French authorities have said.
Health officials said it was an "exceptional case in a severely immunocompromised patient" and there was currently no risk to the public.
Shav is a disease that primarily affects cattle and can be spread by infected midges. Cases have also occurred in sheep, goats, alpacas and horses, but infections in people were previously unheard of.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said they were monitoring the situation, with French officials still investigating how the virus had spread to a human.
It is currently thought the patient contracted Shav through a midge bite in eastern France, the country's health and agriculture ministries said on Thursday, where cases were first identified in animals in the spring.
They said the patient was being treated for a serious illness in a Lyon hospital and experienced neurological complications thought to have been "very likely linked" to the virus, based on initial findings.
The statement stressed that their immune system was weakened, leaving them more vulnerable to getting ill.
"Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans," it noted, having only been identified in animals "despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia".
Dairy herds that catch Shav from bites can experience fever, diarrhoea and poor milk production.
The WHO confirmed this was the first documented human case of the disease.
It said it had not yet made its own formal risk assessment, but advised that current information and knowledge of similar diseases suggested the case was isolated and "unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time".
"Transmissibility of midge-borne viruses also generally declines during the cooler months of the year," it added in a statement.
The ECDC said it was working with French and European partners to investigate the "potential public health implications" of the infection.
The first cases of the virus in Europe were identified in late July, the agency said. It has since been detected in farm animals in several countries, including Ireland, Germany, Italy and Spain, as well as in Jersey.

other-interests-0373036c88.headline: Astronomers unlock a mystery hidden in van Gogh’s The Starry Night
other-interests-0373036c88.fulltext:
Researchers say they’ve identified the constellation depicted in Vincent van Gogh’s famous painting The Starry Night—and that the discovery changes what historians have assumed about the timing of the artwork’s creation.
The painting, now in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York City, is said to date back to mid-June 1889, when van Gogh was in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in France. But astronomers seeking to use the painting’s stars to pin down the exact time and place it was created have reached conflicting conclusions.
In a paper published on October 22 in Scientific Reports, researchers identified the stars in The Starry Night as those of the V-shaped Hyades cluster within the Taurus constellation, as observed on July 22, 1889.
On supporting science journalism

“To my eyes, the star cluster in The Starry Night was the Hyades in Taurus. But earlier studies explained it as Aries,” says space researcher Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, who is first author of the paper. “At that moment, I was sure this painting was worth studying.”
To find the constellation in The Starry Night, the researchers used a software program called Procrustes, which looked for patterns based on the shape formed by the relative positions of a group of stars rather than likely artistic embellishments such as size or color. This “shape analysis” technique matched five stars in the painting with five stars in the Hyades cluster, which had the strongest statistical fit out of any of the alternative constellations tested, including Aries, which had previously been proposed to be the constellation in the center of the painting. The researchers also tested this method on a van Gogh painting with a known constellation in it, the Big Dipper in Starry Night over the Rhône, and found its match had a comparably strong result to that of The Starry Night and Hyades.
To bolster their case, Kim and his colleagues looked to evidence from van Gogh’s letters at the time he was working on The Starry Night to show that perhaps he had painted it in several sessions, with the stars being observed from late July. Although van Gogh mentioned “a new study” of the starry sky in a June 18, 1889, letter, the researchers say that doesn’t mean he had finished the painting. Van Gogh’s letters also make no mention of Aries, despite his regular references to observing Venus, which was close to that constellation in the sky. “The stars of Aries are relatively faint, hardly enough to inspire a painter” at dawn, Kim says, which was when van Gogh often watched the stars.
Another argument against a mid-June date for The Starry Night is the lunar cycle—at that time, the moon would have been in a waning gibbous phase, with its sunlit side appearing as a lopsided oval. Yet the painting shows a waning crescent moon, as it would have been in a late-July sky. Kim also visited Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in June and July 2019 to fully capture van Gogh’s field of view from the precise location where he painted The Starry Night. Kim’s observations there, he says, further confirm the match with the Hyades cluster.
“During this time, van Gogh’s view of the sky was quite restricted” from his window at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole mental asylum, says James Beattie, a Hubble fellow at NASA. “If the identification holds, we can look up today and recognize the same stars van Gogh saw.”
Despite the study’s thoroughness, of course, for a painting as iconic as The Starry Night, there will always be competing versions of an origin story.
“The calculated position of brilliant Venus, in relation to the V shape of the Hyades asterism, does not match the painting,” says Don Olson, a self-proclaimed “celestial sleuth” for astronomical artwork and a professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at Texas State University. The researchers’ conclusions “require strong evidence to overcome Vincent van Gogh’s plain statement that ‘at last I have... a new study of a starry sky’ ... on June 18, 1889.”
Although there are still mysteries to resolve, Kim says the burden of proof has now reversed to proving the painting could not have been made in late July.
“The Starry Night spoke to an astronomer like me,” Kim says. “I listened to its voice.”

other-interests-590a246ab6.headline: Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' depicts the sky on July 22, 1889, researchers find
other-interests-590a246ab6.fulltext:
Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' depicts the sky on July 22, 1889, researchers find
This could be the actual Starry Night.
Researchers think they might have pinpointed the exact night sky that we see depicted in Vincent van Gogh's iconic painting "The Starry Night."
Perhaps one of the most famous paintings in modern history, Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" carries a legacy that continues to inspire and mystify generation after generation. But while you might see in its swirls of color and bright spots of starlight a night sky derived purely from imagination, some scientists think it represents an actual view — one that includes a waning crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades cluster. And they may know exactly when this sky appeared..
In a new study, researchers suggest that "The Starry Night" depicts the pre-dawn sky seen around July 22, 1889 from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where Van Gogh painted it. But while this sky happens to perfectly match the one depicted in the artwork, art historians have long thought that Van Gogh painted this piece in June. Could these findings shift the date of this legendary artwork?
Finding a painted sky
This investigation started decades ago with art historian Albert Boime and astronomer George Abell at UCLA in 1984 and continued in the following years with astronomer Charles Whitney at Harvard University. However, these earlier analyses did not agree with one another, and there was no true consensus about exactly when the sky matched with the painting.
So the question remained, lingering in the minds of those with a shared love for both art and space. And a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of South Korean robotic telescope company SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, picked up the search once more.
"When they see a fragment of a starry sky, observational astronomers like me and amateur astronomers alike will want to solve the puzzle. I am simply someone who pursued that process a little more actively," Kim told Space.com.
But how did Kim's team come to their conclusion, after others had failed to nail down a date over the decades? In short, "we analyzed the painting astronomically, analyzed documents about his situation in July 1889, and then carried out ecological and meteorological investigations," Kim said.
To start with, the team analyzed the sky from the exact location in Saint-Rémy where Van Gogh is said to have painted "The Starry Night." They then used observational geometry to map the historical night sky.
"Modern telescopes are equipped with a function called astrometry, which compares an image of the night sky with celestial coordinates stored in a computer and automatically extracts the coordinates of the image," Kim said. "We used Procrustes analysis, a method that compares only the 'shape' of two sets of points. After matching their position, size and rotation, it measures how similar the two shapes are from the differences that remain (the residuals)."
"Because a star cluster on the canvas may be larger or smaller than in reality and slightly tilted, this method was the right fit. It allowed us to explain, in quantitative terms, what earlier studies had described only qualitatively as 'resembling a certain constellation,'" Kim added.
But this quantitative analysis wasn't enough to say for sure that this was the right-fitting sky, as different constellations could fit to a similar degree, Kim explained. To get closer to their answer, the team combined their analysis with a deep dive through history.
"We also checked whether the stars were actually in that part of the pre-dawn sky on that date, whether they fall within the painter’s field of view, and whether the appearance of the moon and Venus matches the painting. It was the Hyades that satisfied all of these conditions," Kim said.
Exploring astro-art history
As mentioned, the date of this matching sky comes in late July, a month after art historians think Van Gogh painted "The Starry Night." But the researchers suggest that their findings could provide evidence to support the idea that the work was actually painted in July.
Letters written by Van Gogh as early as 1888 describe his desire to paint a star-filled sky. A letter dated April 12, 1888 reads: "A starry sky, for example, well — it’s a thing that I’d like to try to do, just as in the daytime I’ll try to paint a green meadow studded with dandelions."
Kim followed these letters through the months to try and find more information that could potentially alleviate the discrepancy between the matching skies and the actual month the painting was created. Kim pointed to a letter from between late May and early June 1889 that reads: "This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big."
Kim drew on "personal imagination" to find ties between Van Gogh's sky observations in these months and what they might mean for the painting's timeline, Kim shared, so this doesn't definitively change the view of this painting's history. However, Kim suggested that these records could indicate that Van Gogh was repeatedly looking up and watching the pre-dawn sky, which could have led to him seeing this exact sky on July 22.
The painting itself even ignites uncertainty among art historians. As the researchers cite in their new paper, leading art historians see "The Starry Night" as stylistically different from Van Gogh's other works during the month of June, drawing further questions over the date painted.
"What our study shows is that the sky in the painting matches, in both observation and shape, the real pre-dawn sky around July 22. So, what we propose is the possibility that Vincent conceived the idea in June and completed the painting after July 22," Kim said.
However, "I think further research in art history and conservation science could shed more light on this question," Kim added.
This work was described in a study published Oct. 22 in the journal Scientific Reports.
Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. climate-energy-e3be0a54a5.headline: India curtailed 378.52 MU of renewable energy in September 2026
climate-energy-e3be0a54a5.fulltext:
Curtailment during September 2026 affected around 118 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy capacity due to issues such as transmission constraints, limited battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity, and grid flexibility.
In September 2026, 378.52 million units (MU) of variable renewable energy was curtailed, which is equivalent to 1.28 per cent of India’s total renewable energy generation, highlighting ongoing grid integration challenges, JMK Research $ Analytics said.
The curtailment affected a cumulative 118.6 GW of renewable energy capacity, comprising 96.9 GW of solar and 21.7 GW of wind capacity, it added.
“Key reasons for RE curtailment include demand-generation mismatches, transmission constraints, limited storage and grid flexibility, and seasonal overlaps between high renewable output and moderate demand,” it pointed out.
Curtailment surged amid solar capacity additions
Citing data, JMK Research & Analytics said curtailment rose sharply from May to August 2026, reaching nearly four times the level recorded in the same period of 2025. The addition of around 44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY26 has increased pressure on transmission infrastructure and grid flexibility.
Solar power accounted for 83 per cent of September 2026 curtailment, at around 314 MU. However, wind curtailment nearly tripled year on year to 64.98 MU, increasing its share of total curtailment from 4.7 per cent to 17 per cent, it added.
The curtailment remained below 50 MU per month during December 2025-February 2026, but rose from April onwards, peaking at 1,166.52 MU in July. October 2025 recorded the highest curtailment share at 4.32 per cent of the cumulative renewable energy generation.
September curtailment declined month on month
“Curtailment fell 43.31 per cent M-o-M to 378.52 MU in September 2026, down 24 per cent from September 2025. The share of generation curtailed also declined by 0.61 percentage points, from 1.89 per cent in August to 1.28 per cent in September. However, this decline offers seasonal relief rather than evidence of a structural improvement in grid integration,” JMK explained.
Last month, 146.73 MUs (39 per cent) were curtailed due to real-time system constraints, and 231.79 MUs (61 per cent) were curtailed due to Emergency TRAS Down in VRE.
Real-time constraints are back-down instructions issued on the day to manage congestion and operating limits, while emergency TRAS Down involves reducing generation to balance supply and demand. Its use for VRE indicates limited flexibility in the power system to accommodate available renewable generation.
Solar accounted for about 82 per cent of the energy curtailed through TRAS Down, suggesting September’s curtailment was driven mainly by the need to balance the power system rather than grid congestion alone, JMK Research emphasised.
Gujarat and Rajasthan account for nearly 79 per cent
State-wise, Gujarat (187.76 MU, 49.6 per cent) and Rajasthan (110 MU, 29.1 per cent) together accounted for around 79 per cent of the total curtailment.
Gujarat alone contributed about two-thirds of the wind curtailment (43.75 MU), while Rajasthan’s curtailment was entirely solar.
Karnataka and Tamil Nadu recorded technology-wise differences in curtailment, totalling 21.07 MU and 12.93 MU, respectively. Solar accounted for a larger share in Karnataka, while wind contributed more in Tamil Nadu.
Battery storage could help reduce curtailment
BESS can reduce curtailment by storing surplus renewable energy during midday and discharging it during evening peaks. September’s 378.52 MU of curtailment equates to an average of 12.6 (gigawatt-hour) GWh per day, or roughly 3 GW of 4-hour storage as an illustrative scale estimate, JMK Research said.
“Prioritising constrained nodes in Gujarat and Rajasthan, with storage sized to recurring surpluses and responsive to system operator signals, could also help absorb emergency downward reserves (TRAS Down) events,” it suggested.
Published on October 22, 2026
